list.listitem: To treat shoulder pain from suspected subacromial bursitis, rotator cuff impingement including subacromial impingement syndrome, rotator cuff tendinosis, and adhesive capsulitis not responsive to conservative measures such as NSAIDs, rest, and physical therapy.
To assist in diagnosis or exclusion of other causes of shoulder pain.
Note that subacromial and deltoid bursa are synonymous terms.

Steroid injections and physical therapy for shoulder impingement may produce comparable pain and disability outcomes 1 year after starting treatment for patients with unilateral shoulder impingement syndrome. However, the steroid injection group used more healthcare resources after 1 year, based on a small RCT involving 104 adult patients. A prospective, three-arm RCT (N=111) comparing corticosteroid injection (N=36), physiotherapy (N=28), and combined treatment (N=32) for chronic subacromial bursitis reported that corticosteroid injection alone or combined with physiotherapy significantly improved pain (P<0.024) and external rotation (P<0.044) compared to physiotherapy alone, though the physiotherapy group had the lowest recurrence rate at 7.5% versus 36.1% for corticosteroid injection and 17.1% for combined treatment (P<0.001).

A meta-analysis (11 trials, N = 691) reported that corticosteroid injection reduces pain at 4 to 8 weeks in rotator cuff tendinosis (P <0.001, NNT = 5), but not at 8 to 12 weeks post injection (8 trials, N = 564).

For rotator cuff disease less than 6 months duration, a well-designed, 2 x 2 factorial, multicenter, pragmatic RCT evaluating 708 patients concluded that one session of best practice advice with a physiotherapist was comparable to progressive exercise (≤6 sessions), with or without subacromial corticosteroid injection after 12 months, as measured by the Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI). It appears one session of physiotherapy advice may be the most cost-effective approach for non-chronic rotator cuff disorders and that subacromial corticosteroid injection is not effective in the long-term.

In a small RCT (N = 66) the combination of the subacromial corticosteroid injection plus suprascapular nerve block produced pain relief and functional improvement in patients with shoulder impingement syndrome when compared to corticosteroid injection alone.
There is no significant difference in pain relief or functional improvement between the anterior and posterior approach to subacromial bursa injection, based on a small RCT.

A single-blind RCT (N=60) comparing a single intra-bursal injection of platelet-rich plasma (PRP, n=3N) versus triamcinolone acetonide (n=3N) under ultrasonography guidance for shoulder impingement syndrome concluded that corticosteroid injection provided significantly greater short-term pain relief at 1 week (P=0.039), while PRP demonstrated superior long-term improvement in shoulder abduction at 1 year (P=0.012), with no significant difference in pain reduction between the groups beyond the short-term period. However, a double-blind RCT (N=100) comparing subacromial injections of PRP (N=50) versus corticosteroids (N=50) for rotator cuff tendinopathy, finding that PRP provided significantly greater pain relief at 12 months (Visual Analog Scale [VAS] score: 1.68±0.6 vs. 2.3±1.0, P<.001) and superior functional outcomes in the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score (89.8±6.3 vs. 78.0±8.6, P<.001), the Single Assessment Numeric Evaluation (SANE) score (89.2±6.3 vs. 80.5±9.6, P<.001), and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score (2.72±0.6 vs. 4.02±1.7, P<.001), with a lower failure rate (12% vs. 30%, P<.01) compared to corticosteroids​.

A prospective clinical study (N=63) evaluating the difference between anticipated and experienced pain levels in patients undergoing subacromial space (SAS) or glenohumeral joint (GHJ) shoulder injections found that anticipated pain was significantly higher than actual pain experienced (Visual Analog Scale [VAS] score: 6.03 vs. 3.17, P<.001), with GHJ injections rated as more painful than SAS injections (VAS: 3.79 vs. 2.36, P=.05), and 71.42% of patients reporting a decrease in at least one pain category post-injection.

For adhesive capsulitis, one RCT found intra-articular steroid injections to be more effective than oral steroids in improving function, range of motion, and patient satisfaction up to 1 year later. However, a systematic review only found evidence for short-term clinical benefits. Another systematic review evaluating 65 RCTs involving 4097 patients concluded that early use of intraarticular (IA) corticosteroid injection for adhesive capsulitis present for less than a year provided better short-term (≤12 weeks) pain relief and functional improvement compared to no treatment or placebo and physiotherapy alone. Combining IA corticosteroid injection with home exercise program and physiotherapy appears to improve pain in the mid-term (>12 weeks to ≤12 months).
One RCT found that systemic steroid injection was as helpful as injection of a smaller amount of steroid into the joint space.

Based on a Cochrane review, ultrasound-guided injections are not more effective for pain and functional improvement than injections guided by anatomical landmarks, based on moderate-certainty evidence. Additionally, it does not improve quality of life, based on low-certainty evidence. It is unclear if ultrasound-guided injections improve participant-rated treatment success (low-certainty evidence). Furthermore, it does not appear to decrease adverse events (low-certainty evidence). The authors conclude that, given the added cost, ultrasound-guided shoulder injections may not be justified. Another systematic review (N=179) found limited evidence to suggest ultrasound guidance is superior on clinical outcomes compared to landmark-guided injections.
Suspected septic subacromial bursitis.
Active overlying skin infection including cellulitis.
Lack of response to previous injections.
Osteomyelitis.
Breastfeeding is a relative contraindication due to risk of lactation suppression.
Skin preparation material (povidone-iodine, chlorohexidine).
Sterile gloves.
Local anesthesia (1% lidocaine or 0.25% bupivicaine are the most common).
Injectable steroid of choice (triamcinolone and methylprednisone are the most commonly used).
25-gauge 1.5-inch needle and 10 cc syringe. (NOTE: If using a posterior approach, which is not described in this chapter but is used by some physicians, make sure you have an adequate needle length.)
2 x 2 gauze pads, adhesive bandage.
Obtain informed consent from the patient and place patient in seated position on the exam table, with hands resting in their lap.
Identify important anatomic landmarks to locate the subacromial bursa. To do this, apply gentle downward traction on the patient's humerus and palpate the lateral edge of the acromion (see ).
Palpate the soft indentation between the humeral head and the acromion with your thumb to locate the subacromial bursa and mark (optional).
Cleanse skin over subacromial bursa as appropriate.

Apply local anesthesia, if requested by patient, such as ethyl chloride spray or skin wheal of 1% lidocaine with epinephrine. This is usually omitted as patients tolerate the single needle of the steroid injection well.
Prepare the corticosteroid injection of 5 to 7 mL of 1% lidocaine and 20 to 40 mg (1-2 mL) of methylprednisolone or equivalent in a 10 cc syringe.

A 2020 RCT (N = 136) comparing low volume (1mL triamcinolone acetonide/40mg) with high-volume (1ml triamcinolone acetonide with 9mL anesthetic agent) ultrasound guided subacromial injection, demonstrated increased pain relief with the high volume injection across all studied time periods up to 1 year. However a 2023 RCT (N=64) also comparing low volume (1 ml triamcinolone acetonide and 1 ml Lidocaine) subacromial injection injection was non-inferior to high volume (1ml triamcinolone acetonide with 9 ml lidocaine) when assessing pain, ROM, and function using a landmark guided posterior approach.
Advance the 25-gauge needle attached to the medication-containing syringe perpendicular to the skin and deltoid muscle at the previously identified space, aiming towards the opposite nipple.

Keep gently advancing the needle until you appreciate subtle resistance, followed by a sensation of "giving way." This is the penetration of the deltoid muscle fascia and entrance into the subacromial bursa.

Inject the lidocaine/steroid mixture into the space. There should be very little resistance if correctly in bursa. If high resistance or grittiness occurs, the needle may be in the supraspinatus tendon just under and medial to the subacromial bursa. Pull the needle back slightly and redirect until the medication flows freely.

Bicep tendon disorders are found to be associated with rotator cuff tears. An RCT (N = 60) investigated the effect of dual-target subacromial corticosteroid injections where the approach of subacromial bursa injection, as described above, was combined with injection of the proximal biceps long-head tendon, as this has been shown to play a role in impingement syndrome. A dual-target approach may be useful in the setting of reports of less pain at the 3-month follow-up.
Withdraw the needle upon completion of the injection and apply gentle pressure to the injection site with sterile gauze. Cover the area with a bandage.

Retest the patient's shoulder. Increased range of motion and/or strength and diminished pain after injection demonstrates that subacromial impingement or bursitis was likely the cause of the patient's symptoms.
Give discharge instructions including signs of infections, anticipated steroid flare, and need for follow-up.
Post-injection flare (increase in pain 72 hours after injection). Educate your patients that this is common and provide reassurance.
Facial flushing (often resolves within 3-4 days), more common in women.
Failure to enter bursa and place medication in correct space.
Bleeding at injection site or hematoma formation.
Pain at the injection site.
Supraspinatus tendon rupture.
Fat atrophy due to inadvertent subcutaneous steroid injection. This may be avoided by careful placement and withdrawal of needle without subcutaneous injection.
Skin depigmentation.
Cartilage destruction.
Hemarthrosis.
Iatrogenic infection including case reports of septic bursitis occur in less than 1% of injections.

Hyperglycemia. Diabetics should be cautioned for transient, mild elevations in blood glucose levels, however evidence is conflicting. Systemic absorption of corticosteroids is known to occur following intra-articular injections, but is less studied in extra-articular injections such as into a bursa. A recent study has shown that extra-articular injections may cause a transient, clinically insignificant increase in blood glucose. The increase in blood glucose may last 1 to 5 days; for those with poorly controlled diabetes, the increase may be more significant and last longer.
Muscle wasting.
Allergic reaction to the anesthetic agents.
Neurotoxicity from lidocaine in injectate, but this only occurs with plasma levels > 5 mcg/mL.
Lactation suppression.
1 to 2 weeks to reassess symptoms if not resolved.
20610 Arthrocentesis, aspiration and/or injection, major joint or bursa (e.g., shoulder, hip, knee, subacromial bursa).
May return to normal activity as tolerated.
